title: What Do Models Still Suck At? - Peter Gostev, Arena.ai, BullshitBench

primary.label: Evaluation, Testing & Benchmarking
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 99%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is evaluation methodology—introducing the Bullshit Benchmark, analyzing Arena dissatisfaction data, and arguing benchmarks miss real-world model weaknesses. The evaluation spans multiple task categories generally, with substantial software subcategory analysis grounding the coding assistants domain. The content concerns post-deployment evaluation and benchmarking of models already serving users. Requires familiarity with benchmarking concepts and Arena voting mechanics but remains accessible to AI practitioners. A conference presentation analyzing evaluation data and methodology from AI Engineer. Evidence is directly cited from the transcript with specific quantitative claims and methodology descriptions.

summary: Peter Gostev argues that despite benchmark lines relentlessly going up and creating an "AGI-like psychosis," models still have significant weaknesses. He explores this through two lenses: his own "Bullshit Benchmark" and Arena's user dissatisfaction data. The Bullshit Benchmark contains 155 nonsense questions testing whether models push back on false premises or comply. Claude models perform best at rejecting nonsense; GPT and Gemini are roughly 50/50; smaller models almost always comply. Counterintuitively, increased reasoning often makes things worse — models question the premise briefly then spend paragraphs solving the nonsense anyway. Newer and bigger models don't clearly improve except recent Anthropic models. Gostev speculates models are over-trained to solve tasks "at any cost" without learning when to refuse. He then shares Arena data — over 5.5M votes since Q2 2023 across ~700 models. The dislike-both mechanic serves as a dissatisfaction rate: ~17% pre-reasoning, ~12% after o1, ~9% now. To find higher signal, he narrows to ~40,000 expert prompts across top 25 models and subdivides by category. Quantitative tasks (math, physics) showed high dissatisfaction in late 2024/early 2025 then improved dramatically. Creative writing improved but less dramatically. Finance and law showed minimal improvement. Software subcategories reveal uneven progress: overall software dissatisfaction dropped from 23.5% (Q2 2024) to 13% (Q1 2026), but gaming remains notably weak — Gostev notes LLMs produce games with mechanics "all over the place," not interesting or challenging. He attributes some dissatisfaction trends to shifting user expectations, not just model quality: people ask harder questions over time. He closes by arguing benchmarks capture narrow, well-specified tasks but miss the fuzziness and breadth of real white-collar work, urging more effort to improve the bottom of the distribution, not just the frontier.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction: Benchmark Psychosis
sections.summary: Gostev argues that benchmark lines going up create false AGI-like expectations. Arena's own model tracking data confirms the line-goes-up narrative, but he contends this is not the whole story.

sections.title: Bullshit Benchmark: Design and Results
sections.summary: Introduces 155-question benchmark testing whether models push back on nonsense or comply. Claude models perform best, Qwen and Grok are decent, GPT and Gemini are ~50/50, and smaller models almost always comply. Even green-rated responses still show accommodation tendencies.

sections.title: Does Reasoning, Size, or Recency Help?
sections.summary: Analysis shows reasoning often makes nonsense compliance worse — models question the premise briefly then spend paragraphs trying to solve it anyway. No clear pattern for bigger or newer models improving, except recent Anthropic models. Gostev speculates models are over-trained to solve at any cost.

sections.title: Arena Data: Dissatisfaction Rate
sections.summary: Arena has 5.5M+ votes since Q2 2023 across ~700 models. The dislike-both mechanic serves as a dissatisfaction rate: ~17% pre-reasoning, ~12% after o1, ~9% now. Progress is real but 9% remains significant. Gostev begins categorizing prompts to identify which task types drive dissatisfaction.

sections.title: Category-Level Dissatisfaction: Creative, Quantitative, Finance, Law
sections.summary: Creative writing improved but not dramatically. Quantitative tasks (math, physics) had high dissatisfaction in late 2024/early 2025 then dropped dramatically. Finance, law, and 'magical' categories showed minimal improvement with flat lines. Gostev notes user expectations shift over time, making Arena a dynamic benchmark.

sections.title: Expert Software Subcategories: Deep Dive
sections.summary: Narrowing to ~40K expert prompts across top 25 models, Gostev subdivides software into subcategories. Overall software dissatisfaction dropped from 23.5% (Q2 2024) to 13% (Q1 2026). Gaming stands out as persistently weak — LLMs produce games with mechanics all over the place, not interesting or challenging. Gostev notes no good gaming benchmarks exist to capture this.

sections.title: Closing: The Gap Between Benchmarks and Real Work
sections.summary: Gostev argues benchmarks capture narrow, well-specified tasks but miss the fuzziness of real work. He urges improving the bottom of the distribution, not just the frontier. He points to Arena's Hugging Face for shared data, expert prompts, and leaderboards, and invites collaboration.
